title: TSMC CEO Hints Company Could Step In If Intel Cannot Meet Customers’ Advanced Packaging Demand - Stocktwits
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) CEO C.C. Wei hinted during the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker could step in if customers struggle to secure enough advanced-packaging supply from Intel (INTC). The remarks came after Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan asked whether TSMC would support customers that initially chose Intel’s EMIB-T packaging technology but later faced supply constraints, according to the Koyfin transcript of the company’s third-quarter (Q3) earnings call. “I try to avoid answering it directly, but let me say that, yes, we will be,” Wei said. “Number one priority I already indicated is that TSMC’s customer’s product can be introduced into the market smoothly. That’s a number one priority. Okay? And that gives you enough of a hint.” TSM stock fell nearly 4% in morning trade amid broader market weakness as concerns around AI spending and hotter-than-expected producer prices weighed on markets. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment behind the chip supplier to companies like Nvidia (NVDA) and Apple (AAPL), improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Platform data showed a 666% increase in chatter in the same time period. Intel’s EMIB-T and TSMC’s Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) are competing approaches to advanced packaging that connect chip components and high-bandwidth memory into integrated systems used in AI computing. A shortage of packaging capacity can delay deliveries even when the underlying chips are available. Should that happen, clients can either delay their launch or switch to a different supplier. During Intel’s second-quarter (Q2) earnings call in July, CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated that  EMIB-T orders were growing and yield and reliability targets were being met, with the company preparing to scale production to support customers’ 2027 ramps. INTC stock fell over 5% in morning trade on Thursday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the company continued to trend in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day. Wei said TSMC is already producing packages five times the standard reticle size, with plans to expand to nine times and eventually 14 times that size. “We are in the real-world production of 5x reticle size. I don’t believe that anybody can do that today except at TSMC, and the yield is excellent,” he said. “So our customers are very satisfied with the result.” Wei added that the company is also working to reduce packaging costs, stating that its CoWoS technology remains customers’ preferred option. TSM stock fell in morning trade on Thursday despite reporting a Q3 earnings and revenue beat. Earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.91, according to Koyfin, beating Wall Street expectations of $0.89 per share. Revenue rose 50% year-over-year to $46.12 billion, beating analysts’ forecast of $45.69 billion. This was the company’s sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings. It forecast fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue would rise as much as 61% as compared to a year ago. TSM stock has gained over 36% this year. It’s currently trading around 14% below its record high of over $487 seen earlier this month. Microsoft (MSFT) is drawing fresh analyst attention on Thursday ahead of its upcoming earnings report, with four firms raising their price targets on the stock. According to The Fly, TD Cowen, Mizuho, Citi and UBS raised their Microsoft price targets, citing Azure trends, cloud demand and enterprise AI adoption. MSFT stock traded nearly 0.5% higher at the time of writing. According to The Fly, TD Cowen raised its price target on Microsoft to $625 from $540 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating. The firm updated its model ahead of quarterly results, seeing the potential for a “higher than normal” beat on Azure as the third-party data it tracks screened strongest in history, alongside a full quarter of Fairwater and a bullish read on an OpenAI growth inflection. Mizuho analyst Gregg Moskowitz raised the firm’s price target to $600 from $510 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating. Moskowitz said Mizuho’s channel checks in Q3 were “very healthy overall,” with strong public cloud and consumption data points and AI adoption remaining robust. Citi analyst Tyler Radke raised the firm’s price target to $636 from $600 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating, according to The Fly. Citi said its recent chief investment officer survey and reseller checks reinforced its view that Microsoft’s core productivity and public cloud franchise should accelerate as enterprises increase AI spending. The analyst also considers Microsoft among the best-positioned AI vendors. Meanwhile, UBS analyst Karl Keirstead raised the price target on the stock to $675 from $525 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating. He said the stock’s 39% rally had raised growth expectations, but Azure and Microsoft 365 fundamentals supported the optimism and the valuation remained reasonable. Separately, UMass Memorial Health announced a multi-year initiative with Microsoft and Accenture (ACN) to modernize its data platform using Microsoft Azure. The unified platform is intended to replace siloed reporting systems and support more advanced analytics. The initiative will also move UMass Memorial’s electronic health record to Azure, connecting clinical, operational and research data on one platform. The health system aims to use the connected data to advance quality and safety goals, including reducing patient length of stay and caregivers’ administrative burden. Accenture will introduce agentic AI tools to automate complex workflows and uncover insights. UMass Memorial Health expects the transformation to improve speed, quality and security while lowering long-term infrastructure costs. SpaceX (SPCX) continued to increase its foothold in the commercial aviation market, with United Airlines (UAL) announcing that Starlink satellite internet service is now available on nearly half of the carrier’s daily flights. The development comes just a week after American Airlines (AAL) announced plans to equip its entire mainline fleet with Starlink. SPCX shares were down about 4% at the time of writing, tracking weakness in the broader space and the tech sector. UAL stock edged marginally higher. United Airlines said Starlink is now installed on more than 635 aircraft. According to a July SEC filing by United, the airline operates 1,579 mainline and regional aircraft. United is adding Starlink to about 20 planes per week and expects to complete installations by the end of 2027. United also launched a Starlink Tracker, allowing travelers to check whether their flights offer the service. Last week, American Airlines announced plans to install Starlink on more than 1,030 aircraft. Installations are expected to begin in early 2027, covering both narrowbody and widebody aircraft. Starlink is also available in 38% of Alaska Air Group’s (ALK) fleet. Alaska Air operates Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. Globally, Qatar Airways already offers Starlink Wi-Fi on 150 widebody aircraft, while Air France is targeting a fleetwide rollout by year-end. Emirates is also set to launch the service. Starlink has also been in the news since SpaceX announced a deal last week to acquire Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz wireless spectrum portfolio. The deal would see SpaceX expand its Starlink Mobile service by combining satellite connectivity with ground-based mobile networks, potentially increasing competition with traditional telecom operators. Intuit (INTU) is expanding its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities with a deal to acquire Sequence, a startup that automates billing, contracts and revenue recognition for businesses. The acquisition, announced Thursday, will add new capabilities to QuickBooks Online Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite as the company looks to capture a larger share of the mid-market financial software business. Financial terms were not disclosed.At the time of this writing, INTU stock traded up more than 4%. Sequence's platform automates the quote-to-revenue process, covering everything from pricing and customer contracts to invoicing, collections and revenue recognition. Its AI agents are designed to take over routine finance tasks. The acquisition comes as usage-based and hybrid pricing models create additional work for finance teams, which must track customer contracts, changing consumption and revenue recognition across multiple systems. “Revenue management has long been the most fragmented workflow in the back office,” said Sequence Co-Founder and CEO Riya Grover. The deal would allow Intuit to bring those capabilities into its existing financial software products rather than leaving customers to manage revenue processes across separate applications. Intuit has been investing in AI-powered financial tools to attract businesses with more complex accounting needs. In August, the company expanded its Intuit Intelligence platform across QuickBooks Online Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite, introducing conversational AI tools that help finance teams analyze business data, identify discrepancies and automate accounting workflows. The latest acquisition would extend that automation beyond bookkeeping and reporting into the revenue cycle itself. The mid-market push comes against a backdrop of growing business software revenue. Intuit's Global Business Solutions revenue increased 16% year over year to $12.9 billion in fiscal 2026. At its September investor day, the company reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 companywide revenue guidance of $23.28 billion to $23.51 billion, representing 9% to 10% growth. Intuit also expects Global Business Solutions revenue of $13.07 billion to $13.16 billion under its revised reporting structure, which excludes Mailchimp. Apollo Global Management (APO) Chief Economist Torsten Slok stated that the Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy choice as producer prices accelerate and consumers begin pulling back on spending, raising the risk of an uncomfortable mix of persistent inflation and slowing economic growth. “This is a definition of stagflation,” Slok said during a CNBC interview. “We have higher prices, and in response to higher prices, we buy less.” His comments came after U.S. producer price inflation accelerated sharply in August, defying expectations for a decline. The annual producer price index (PPI) rose to 6.3%, its second-highest level in four years, higher than the expected 5.5%. Monthly headline PPI climbed 1.3%, more than double the 0.6% increase economists had expected. Core PPI also exceeded expectations, with the monthly reading coming in at 0.7% against an estimate of 0.3%. U.S. equities traded lower ahead of the PPI data release. After markets opened, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were on track to hit their worst week since June. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.4%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 1.3%. Meanwhile, SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) stayed in the green, with gains of around 0.44%. SPY and QQQ were among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Retail sentiment around QQQ  shifted to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, while chatter increased to’high’ from ‘normal’ levels. According to Slok, the hotter inflation reading complicates the Fed’s efforts to balance price stability against the risk of slowing growth. Slok said policymakers must decide whether to prioritize rising inflation or signs that consumers are beginning to rein in spending. “The challenge for the Fed is: Should they be focusing on inflation going up, or should they be focusing on the slowdown in consumers’ money and the risk of GDP growth?” he said. Slok pointed to housing and autos as early examples of interest-rate-sensitive sectors responding to tighter financial conditions. Mortgage rates have climbed substantially from their pandemic-era lows, while financing and leasing a car have become more expensive. “The more interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy are beginning to respond,” Slok said. “We’re seeing that in housing. We’re seeing that in autos.” He added that consumers are also showing early signs of adjusting their spending as higher prices squeeze household budgets. Slok also warned that the U.S. economy has become increasingly dependent on AI investment, leaving growth vulnerable if companies slow spending on data centers and related infrastructure. “GDP growth is normally two [percent], and now roughly one percentage point of GDP is coming from the AI spending boom,” he said. A slowdown in the build-out could weigh on economic growth even without triggering a recession. The key question, Slok said, is whether the financial returns from AI investment arrive as quickly as investors expect. “What if that payoff does not arrive with the speed that the consensus was expecting?” he said. Slok expects some moderation in data center construction as expectations for earnings and investment returns adjust, but does not anticipate a recession. “I think the answer is that we will not get a recession, but I do think we’ll get some more dampening of the data center build-out,” he said. With PPI inflation at its second-highest level in four years, CME FedWatch data put the odds of a Fed rate hike at 27.1% in October. Penske Automotive Group (PAG) shares rallied around 8% in premarket trading on Thursday after the company agreed to be taken private by Penske Corporation and Mitsui & Co. in a deal valuing the company at approximately $16.3 billion. Roger Penske, chair and CEO of Penske Automotive Group, called the transaction “an important next chapter for PAG,” saying the company would work with Mitsui to build on its operational excellence, drive innovation and expand its business through new opportunities and collaborative projects. Under the agreement, PAG shareholders will receive $212 per share in cash, excluding Penske Corporation, Mitsui & Co. and other members of the investor group. The offer represents an 8.84% premium to PAG’s closing price on Oct. 14, the last trading day before the deal was announced. The deal will be carried out through Motown Acquisition Corp., an entity owned by Penske Corporation and Mitsui. Upon completion, Penske will own approximately 64% of the privately held company, while Mitsui will hold the remaining 36%. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and shareholder votes. Approval requires a majority of outstanding shares entitled to vote, as well as a majority of votes cast by unaffiliated shareholders. Once the transaction closes, PAG shares will no longer trade on the New York Stock Exchange. Penske Automotive is set to report its third-quarter results before the market opens on Oct. 28. Analysts tracked by Fiscal AI expect revenue of $8.39 billion and earnings per share of $3.46. Separately, Penske Automotive’s board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $1.46 per share, up $0.02, or 1.4%, from the previous payout. The dividend represents an annualized rate of $5.84 per share and is payable on Dec. 1 to shareholders of record on Nov. 13, 2026. title: Robust AI demand drove Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US) to exceed earnings expectations, leading Wall Street analysts to collectively raise their target prices, with some reaching as high as $600. - 富途牛牛
content: Taiwan Semiconductor's robust growth prospects have prompted Wall Street firms such as Needham and Susquehanna to raise their price targets, while Bernstein has reiterated its "outperform" rating and maintained a $554 price target. Zhitong Finance APP learned that Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US), the world's largest wafer foundry, reported third-quarter 2026 results and fourth-quarter guidance that both exceeded market expectations, further easing investors' concerns about a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending. Taiwan Semiconductor's management stated that, for now, there are no signs of cooling demand for AI, and customer demand for advanced-node chips still far outstrips the company's supply capacity. Strong growth prospects have prompted Wall Street firms such as Needham and Susquehanna to raise their price targets, while Bernstein has reiterated its "Outperform" rating and maintained a $554 price target. According to a research report released by Bernstein on October 15, Taiwan Semiconductor's third-quarter revenue reached NT$1.494 trillion, up 17.6% quarter over quarter, exceeding the market's expectation of NT$1.473 trillion; net profit stood at NT$763.1 billion, up 8% quarter over quarter, also surpassing market forecasts. Earnings per share came in at NT$29.43, higher than the market's estimate of NT$28.91. However, affected by the ramp-up of 2-nanometer advanced-process capacity and overseas expansion, Taiwan Semiconductor's third-quarter gross margin fell from 67.7% in the previous quarter to 66.4%, slightly below the market's expectation of 67.1%. Its operating profit margin also declined from 60.3% to 58.7%. Despite a decline in profit margins, Bernstein believes that Taiwan Semiconductor's results still reflect strong market demand and excellent execution. The short-term pressure on gross margins is partly due to capacity ramp-up costs resulting from stronger-than-expected demand for the 2-nanometer process. Even more encouraging for the market is Taiwan Semiconductor's outlook for future growth. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to reach between US$52.3 billion and US$54.3 billion, significantly above the market's prior consensus estimate of around US$50.5 billion. Based on the midpoint of this guidance, fourth-quarter revenue is expected to increase by approximately 14% quarter over quarter, markedly stronger than typical seasonal trends. Meanwhile, Taiwan Semiconductor has raised its full-year 2026 U.S. dollar revenue growth forecast from slightly above 40% to 44%, indicating that demand for AI chips continues to drive the company's accelerated performance growth. AI demand continues to far outstrip supply capacity, with advanced-node capacity expansion accelerating. Taiwan Semiconductor CEO C. C. Wei stated during the earnings call that there are currently no signs of a slowdown in AI demand. Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson noted that Taiwan Semiconductor's management described current AI demand as "extremely strong," adding that the company not only continues to engage with its customers but has also dispatched teams to conduct on-site assessments of U.S. data center construction progress and power supply conditions, in order to evaluate the sustainability of AI infrastructure expansion. Taiwan Semiconductor's investigation shows that construction progress is currently proceeding smoothly overall, while customer demand remains significantly higher than the capacity the company can provide. Notably, Taiwan Semiconductor had previously projected that the compound annual growth rate of AI accelerator-related revenue would reach the mid-to-high 50% range from 2024 to 2029. This time, management further indicated that the actual growth rate could exceed the earlier forecast. Needham analyst Charles Shi believes that this statement suggests the AI chip market still holds growth potential beyond current expectations. In addition to AI accelerators, Taiwan Semiconductor also highlighted the growing demand for central processing units (CPUs) and networking chips. Bernstein notes that the widespread adoption of AI agents and open-source models is boosting the efficiency of AI applications, lowering the barriers to entry for businesses adopting AI technologies, and thereby driving expanded demand for advanced manufacturing processes. At the same time, the CPU computing power required by AI agents, along with the ever-growing need for network connectivity between data centers, is emerging as a new engine of growth. Based on its third-quarter performance, Taiwan Semiconductor's high-performance computing (HPC) segment posted a 22% quarter-over-quarter revenue increase, while its smartphone business grew by 10%, the IoT segment expanded by 5%, and the automotive electronics segment surged by 23%. Bernstein data shows that in the third quarter, revenue from the high-performance computing business reached approximately $32 billion, accounting for 68% of the company's total revenue, while the share of smartphone business revenue has dropped to 21%, highlighting that AI and high-performance computing are increasingly becoming Taiwan Semiconductor's most important growth engines. 2-nanometer production capacity is expected to double next year, with capital expenditures likely to rise further. Faced with the continuously growing demand for advanced processes, Taiwan Semiconductor is accelerating its global capacity expansion. Susquehanna analyst Mehdi Hosseini noted that Taiwan Semiconductor expects its annual production capacity for the 2-nanometer process to more than double by 2027. Bernstein's research report shows that the 2-nanometer process accounted for approximately 8% of Taiwan Semiconductor's wafer revenue in the third quarter, reflecting that this latest process is rapidly entering the commercial mass-production phase. As for the 3-nanometer process, Taiwan Semiconductor plans to add four new fabs, with two located in Taiwan, one in the United States, and the other in Japan. Susquehanna noted that Taiwan Semiconductor will also add a 3-nanometer fab in Tainan, Taiwan, with mass production expected to begin in the first half of 2028; additionally, another plant is already slated to start production in the first half of 2027. The U.S. expansion plan is also being accelerated. Taiwan Semiconductor's second fab in Arizona is expected to begin mass production in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of the original schedule. Meanwhile, the company is evaluating the construction of a new manufacturing facility in Texas. In terms of more advanced process technologies, Taiwan Semiconductor's A14 process is scheduled to begin risk production in 2027 and enter mass production in 2028. Susquehanna reports that the current early-stage development progress of this process is even faster than that of the 2-nanometer process at a similar stage. Advanced packaging technologies are also continuously advancing. Taiwan Semiconductor currently has the production capacity for advanced packaging at five times the mask size and is moving toward even larger packaging specifications—nine times and fourteen times the mask size—to meet the future demand of AI chips for higher computing power and greater package area. On the capital expenditure front, Taiwan Semiconductor is keeping its 2026 investment plan of US$60 to 64 billion unchanged, but management emphasized that capital spending from 2026 to 2028 will increase significantly compared with the past three years, and the growth rate could expand further. Needham forecasts that Taiwan Semiconductor's capital expenditures will reach US$90 billion in 2027 and further increase to US$100 billion in 2028, to support additional 3-nanometer capacity and potential expansion plans in Texas. Bernstein believes that despite the continued rise in capital expenditures, as revenue growth accelerates, Taiwan Semiconductor's capital expenditure as a percentage of revenue is still expected to decline gradually. In addition, Bernstein's research report mentions discussions between Taiwan Semiconductor and Tesla (TSLA.US) CEO Elon Musk regarding the Terafab fab. Taiwan Semiconductor confirmed that the two sides had engaged in communications but emphasized that the fab must be operated independently by Taiwan Semiconductor. Based on this, Bernstein concludes that it may be difficult for the two parties to reach a cooperation agreement; however, whether the new plant in Texas is related to this project remains unclear at this time. Wall Street raises price targets, with some analysts setting a high of $600. Strong financial performance and expansion prospects have prompted several Wall Street firms to turn increasingly bullish on Taiwan Semiconductor. Needham maintains a "Buy" rating on Taiwan Semiconductor and raises its price target from $530 to $560. Analyst Charles Shi notes that 2027 could be a pivotal year for Taiwan Semiconductor, as it sets a new revenue record while sustaining rapid growth. Susquehanna has sharply raised Taiwan Semiconductor's price target from $430 to $600. The firm believes that the expansion of 2-nanometer and 3-nanometer production capacity, upgrades in advanced packaging technologies, and accelerated progress in building a U.S. manufacturing base will further strengthen Taiwan Semiconductor's competitive edge in the global advanced wafer foundry market. Wedbush also reiterated its "outperform" rating, believing that Taiwan Semiconductor's assessment of AI demand is highly credible, particularly since the company has already factored data center power, memory chips, and other potential supply-chain bottlenecks into its demand forecast. Bernstein, meanwhile, maintains a price target of $554 for Taiwan Semiconductor's U.S. shares and a "Outperform" rating, implying roughly 29% upside from its October 15 closing price of about $430. The firm also keeps its price target of NT$3,300 for Taiwan Semiconductor's Taiwan-listed shares, which, compared with the day's closing price of NT$2,440, suggests an upside potential of approximately 35%. Bernstein forecasts that Taiwan Semiconductor's earnings per share will reach $17.18 in 2026 and further rise to $22.48 in 2027. The firm notes that, compared with three months ago, the demand environment facing Taiwan Semiconductor has improved markedly, and the company's prudent capacity expansion and efficient execution in consistently meeting customer needs are expected to drive long-term compound earnings growth. However, not all institutions share the same optimistic outlook on Taiwan Semiconductor. Jeff Pu, an analyst at GF Securities, believes that Taiwan Semiconductor's third-quarter results were broadly in line with expectations or slightly below, and therefore maintains a "Hold" rating. The firm forecasts that, driven by sustained demand for AI accelerators, CPUs, and networking chips, as well as moderate price hikes across both advanced and mature process nodes, Taiwan Semiconductor's revenue could grow 39% year over year in 2027. However, the firm also cautioned that the ramp-up of 2-nanometer and A14 process capacities, overseas expansion, and rising equipment costs could offset some of the margin improvements driven by revenue growth, leaving Taiwan Semiconductor's gross margins relatively stable overall from 2027 to 2028. In addition, GF Securities believes that Intel's (INTC.US) EMIB-T advanced packaging technology still poses competition to Taiwan Semiconductor's CoWoS technology. Notably, despite Taiwan Semiconductor posting strong financial results and raising its full-year growth outlook, its U.S. shares still fell more than 2% in early trading on Thursday, reflecting that investors' concerns about AI‑sector valuations, capital expenditures, and potential investment returns have yet to subside. Shares of Intel and GlobalFoundries (GFS.US) also declined by more than 2%, indicating overall pressure on the semiconductor sector. However, Bernstein believes that Taiwan Semiconductor's latest earnings send a clear signal: AI infrastructure development has not yet shown any significant slowdown, demand for advanced processes continues to outstrip supply, and Taiwan Semiconductor is consolidating its pivotal role in the global AI chip supply chain through ongoing capacity expansion. A record report from the world’s largest dedicated semiconductor foundry isn’t stopping the selling, and the weakness is spreading across chip names. Meanwhile, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock is at $94.33, down 4% and sliding more faster than Taiwan Semiconductor stock. Also, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is at $552.98, down 3% and falling in step with Taiwan Semiconductor stock. For a sector-level read, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is at $504.75, down 3%. At the same time, the broader tech fund Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is at $720.55, down 1%, so semiconductors are falling harder than the large-cap technology benchmark. Taiwan Semiconductor reported its Q3 2026 results with revenue and net income both sharply higher than a year earlier, extending its record-profit streak to a sixth straight quarter. The results beat estimates on demand tied to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Its current-quarter sales guidance also landed above what analysts had modeled. On the earnings call, Chief Executive Officer C.C. Wei stated that demand for Taiwan Semiconductor’s leading-edge technologies remains extremely robust, pointing to rising adoption of agentic AI. “The AI market continues to be very strong,” Wei declared, adding, “We did not see any sign of slowdown.” One soft spot sits in gross margin, which narrowed from the preceding quarter. Taiwan Semiconductor builds the advanced processors other companies design, so its results read as a demand signal for the whole chip complex. The company pioneered the pure-play foundry model and manufactures for fabless designers and integrated device manufacturers, with fabs across Asia, Europe, and North America. Advanced packaging extends Taiwan Semiconductor’s reach beyond wafers, and management described chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) packaging as customers’ top choice. A partnership on silicon interposers is also aimed at easing a significant backend shortage. Intel takes a different path, designing and fabricating its own chips across a manufacturing footprint in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. Its Intel Foundry business also offers process technologies and advanced packaging to outside customers. AMD represents the other end of the spectrum, leaving manufacturing to foundries while it designs server processors, graphics chips, and AI accelerators. Skeptics of Taiwan Semiconductor stock point to the fact that shares ran hard into the report and had already priced in a good quarter. Selling into a record result fits that pattern, and the narrower gross margin gives skeptics a fresh talking point. Management attributed the decline primarily to dilution from the initial ramp of its newest process node. Overseas fabs add further cost pressure, though productivity gains and capacity optimization across nodes provide a partial offset. Taiwan Semiconductor’s capital spending is also set to climb well above recent levels, and management said, “If we do our job right, the increase in revenue will outpace the increase in CAPEX.” Demand still exceeding supply anchors the bull case. Wei said, “Based on our assessed demand, we still think the demand is higher than the supply, and we are working very hard to narrow the gap.” That pull is broadening with the shift “from chatbot to AI assistants,” and capacity expansion in Taiwan, Arizona, and Japan gives the company room to capture more of it (we highlighted seven non-chipmaker suppliers riding the same buildout, from power to cooling, in a free AI infrastructure report). Taiwan Semiconductor’s next quarterly report could show whether its margin trajectory holds as capital spending rises. Management expects dilution from overseas fabs to widen in the next few years as more U.S. capacity comes online. For the iShares Semiconductor ETF, the open variable is the market’s appetite for AI hardware after record results from the sector’s bellwether foundry failed to steady chip stocks.                         Patricia Miller TSMC reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of NT$1,494.24 billion, up 50.9% from a year earlier, with Q4 revenue guided at US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion. TSMC's profit grew faster than its sales in the third quarter, with net income up 68.7% on a 50.9% revenue gain as chips made at 7 nanometers and below reached 79% of wafer revenue. Management expects advanced-process demand and the 2-nanometer ramp-up to lift fourth-quarter revenue, though currency moves and execution remain risks. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (TWSE: 2330) (NYSE: TSM) reported third-quarter net income of NT$763.06 billion on Oct. 15, an increase of 68.7% from the same quarter a year earlier. The Hsinchu, Taiwan-based company released the results for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. TSMC manufactures chips that other companies design, a business model known as a pure-play foundry. Chip designers use its factories to produce processors for products ranging from smartphones to data center servers, and the company's quarterly results are followed closely across the semiconductor supply chain. Consolidated revenue reached NT$1,494.24 billion in the third quarter, up 50.9% from NT$989.92 billion a year earlier. TSMC prepared all figures under TIFRS, Taiwan's version of international financial reporting standards, on a consolidated basis. Diluted earnings per share rose 68.7% to NT$29.43, compared with NT$17.44 in the third quarter of 2025. Each American depositary receipt unit, the form in which TSMC shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange, earned US$4.60. Measured in US dollars, third-quarter revenue was $46.72 billion, up 41.2% year over year. The gap between growth in New Taiwan dollars and growth in US dollars reflects exchange rate movements between the two currencies over the period. Compared with the second quarter of 2026, revenue rose 17.6% in New Taiwan dollars and 16.2% in US dollars. The sequential increase followed second-quarter revenue of NT$1,270.38 billion. Net income rose 8% from the second quarter, a slower pace than revenue growth over the same period. Income before tax increased 5.6% quarter over quarter to NT$911.04 billion, and net profit margin for the third quarter was 51.1%. TSMC groups its manufacturing by process size, measured in nanometers. Smaller numbers refer to newer processes that place more transistors on each chip. The company defines 7-nanometer and smaller processes as advanced technologies, and these made up 79% of wafer revenue in the quarter. The 3-nanometer process was the largest single contributor, accounting for 33% of total wafer revenue. It was followed by the 5-nanometer process at 28% and the 7-nanometer process at 10%. The 2-nanometer process, TSMC's newest, accounted for 8% of total wafer revenue in the third quarter. The company identified this process as a source of growth heading into the final quarter of the year. Gross margin, the share of revenue left after direct production costs, was 66.4% in the quarter. Gross profit rose 68.6% from a year earlier to NT$992.38 billion. Operating margin was 58.7%. Income from operations, which subtracts operating expenses such as research and administration, increased 75% year over year to NT$876.45 billion. "Our business in the third quarter was supported by strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies," Wendell Huang, Senior VP and Chief Financial Officer, TSMC, said in the earnings release. Leading-edge, in TSMC's usage, refers to its most advanced manufacturing processes. In advanced contract chipmaking, TSMC competes directly with the foundry business of Samsung Electronics and with Intel's foundry unit. Both offer advanced manufacturing processes to outside chip designers, placing them in the same direct category as TSMC. Same news, different lens. TSMC said it expects fourth-quarter revenue of between US$52.3 billion and US$54.3 billion. The midpoint of that range, US$53.3 billion, would be about 14% higher than third-quarter US dollar revenue of $46.72 billion. The company expects gross margin of between 65% and 67%, based on an assumed exchange rate of 31.8 New Taiwan dollars per US dollar. That range brackets the 66.4% gross margin reported for the third quarter. Operating margin is forecast at 56.5% to 58.5%, using the same exchange rate assumption. The top of that range sits slightly below the 58.7% operating margin the company reported for the third quarter. Huang said TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business "to be supported by continued strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology." A ramp-up refers to the period in which a new process moves from early output to higher-volume production. The company noted that its third-quarter figures have not been approved by its Board of Directors. Its margin forecasts depend on the stated exchange rate assumption, so movements in the New Taiwan dollar against the US dollar could affect reported results. Management expects continued demand for its most advanced processes and the 2-nanometer ramp-up to support fourth-quarter revenue of up to US$54.3 billion, though currency movements, the pace of new production, and broader chip demand remain key risks to that outlook. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) reported blockbuster third-quarter results, driven by robust demand for advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and high-performance computing (HPC). However, TSM stock fell sharply after the results. Revenue rose 16.2% sequentially and reached $46.72 billion, comfortably above analyst estimates of $45.41 billion. At the same time, earnings per share (EPS) came in at $ 4.60, beating expectations of $4.42 by about 4.1%. Despite the earnings beat, however, profitability showed signs of near-term trouble. Namely, gross margin declined 130 basis points from the previous quarter to 66.4%, while operating margin stood at 58.7%. As investors weighed the company’s aggressive expansion plans, rising capital expenditures, and mounting pressure on profit margins, TSM shares closed the session at $430, down 3.4% from the previous close. The price then fell another 2.1% to $420.98 in after-hours trading, leaving the shares approximately 5.5% below the previous closing price overall. The decline appears to suggest that investors are looking beyond earnings figures, focusing instead on the margins, future capital requirements, and the costs associated with international manufacturing expansion. While TSMC shares remain within the upper half of their reported 52-week range of roughly $266-$487, the market reaction indicates that strong AI demand might not be sufficient to ease concerns about the company’s growth strategy. Management itself attributed the pressure partly to the ramp-up of its next-generation 2-nanometer manufacturing technology and the continued expansion of overseas fabrication facilities. However, C.C. Wei, TSMC’s chairman and chief executive, still stressed the company’s expansion plans are going “full speed ahead:” “We are moving full speed ahead to increase our capacity to meet our assessed demand, and stepping up our CapEx investment to support our customers’ future growth,” Wei said. While confident, Wei’s tone probably did little to alleviate investor concerns, most of which were, as mentioned, focused primarily on unchecked expansion efforts. For now, then, management remains confident that demand will support further expansion, while the market worries whether TSMC can sustain its growth while managing the near-term costs. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3-$54.3 billion, implying approximately 14% sequential growth and 58% growth compared with the same period a year earlier. In addition, the company expects gross margin to range between 65% and 67%, while operating margin is projected at 56.5% to 58.5%. As for full-year 2026 results, management expects revenue to grow by approximately 44% and reaffirms its capital expenditure budget of 60-64 billion. However, TSMC expects capital spending between 2026 and 2028 to be significantly higher than during the preceding three years, which is another reason the shares took a hit. After all, the expansion includes a substantial increase in next-generation manufacturing capacity. More specifically, TSMC expects its 2-nanometer capacity to double in 2027. content: U.S. stock futures were mixed early on Thursday as a broad selloff in global tech stocks and a hotter-than-expected CPI inflation print weighed on investor sentiment. Concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending, combined with rising bond yields and Fed rate hike fears, have kept the market cautious. Asian markets took a knock, with South Korea’s KOSPI plunging over 7% and triggering a trading halt, led by a crack in heavyweights Samsung and SK Hynix. As of 4 a.m. ET, Nasdaq futures fell 1%, S&P 500 futures were down 0.3%, while Dow and Russell 2000 futures gained 0.4%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 Index, has moderated to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ a day ago, while Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, has remained ‘bullish’ despite the selloff in semiconductor stocks. On Wednesday, the inflation print showed September CPI rising 0.6% month-on-month and 3.7% year-on-year, coming in above street estimates. With 10-year Treasury yields hovering around 5%, CME Fedwatch now puts expectations for a Fed rate hike at the upcoming October meeting at 27%. Investors will be watching for the release of September Producer Price Index (PPI), retail sales, and weekly jobless claims data today. More importantly, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak at the IMF meeting later today. His commentary could offer clues on how policymakers are assessing the current macroeconomic situation. Noted investor Michael Burry has warned of long-lasting market pain, as falling Treasury yields do not guarantee an equity rally. He added that semiconductors have already seen a selloff along with yields, and now a similar move across the Mag 7 stocks could add conviction to his ‘Red October’ call. A new Gartner report has raised warnings, saying that over $3.5 trillion in AI infra spending faces write-down risks by 2030, and that over 80% of neocloud providers could lose their independent operations. This sparked a rout across AI cloud stocks on Wednesday. CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS) continue to see sharp dips along with other neocloud peers, even as CoreWeave CEO reaffirmed confidence in the company’s $99B backlog. Additionally, Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment bought 189K shares on Wednesday. And Dan Ives stated that the fears around Coreweave’s selloff were “way overdone.” Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSM): Shares fell over 2% in early premarket trade despite raising its 2026 revenue guidance and posting a record Q3 profit. Micron Technology (MU): Shares reel under pressure in early premarket trading amid global memory weakness. Separately, reports suggest the Taiwan President has urged management and unions to resolve bonus disputes to avoid a strike at Micron’s Taiwan HBM packaging hub. SK Hynix (SKHY): Shares have slipped for the eighth session amid reports that the company is seeking U.S. approval to export American chipmaking equipment to Chinese facilities as a precondition for building a factory in the U.S. Nvidia (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), and Qualcomm (QCOM) are also in the red, tracking broad-based weakness across the sector and amid reports that ByteDance is in advanced talks with MediaTek about custom AI data center chips. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) fell over 2%. Tesla (TSLA): Shares fell nearly 2% in early premarket trade ahead of its Roadster event, which CEO Elon Musk has promised will be the ‘greatest product demo of all time’. Retail is also tracking a Barclays note that suggested a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger announcement is likely before Tesla’s annual meeting that takes place in early December. SpaceX (SPCX): Elon Musk claims that the company’s valuation could top $100 trillion within 10 years. AST SpaceMobile (ASTS): Shares fell 4% in early premarket trade, tracking broader sector weakness. Meanwhile, analysts have highlighted timeline risks suggesting that the company’s 60-satellite milestone could slip to 2028. Rocket Labs (RKLB) shares fell 10% in early premarket trade, and retail sentiment on Stocktwits fell to an all-time low after the company announced a delay of its reusable Neutron rocket launch to 2027. ImmunityBio (IBRX) shares rose 2% in early premarket trade after the FDA expanded approval of its immunotherapy drug, Anktiva, for papillary non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. Jefferies raised the firm’s price target to $14 from $12 and maintained a Buy call, noting that the approval came about three months ahead of the January 2027 PDUFA deadline. Skydance (SKYD) remains on the retail radar after clarifying an NYSE reference price adjustment to its Class B warrants, reducing the overall common valuation to $45.6 billion. Netflix (NFLX) shares held steady in early premarket, even as retail sentiment on Stocktwits dipped into ‘bearish’ territory ahead of its earnings report next week. Fiscal support is clearly cushioning the economy, but household financing remains weak and endogenous momentum still needs repair. Monetary easing remains the broad direction, with attention on whether property sales can stabilize. CoreWeave shares fell over 15% overnight, its bonds slumped into distressed territory, and CDS pricing implies a five-year default probability of 63%. Total debt plus lease obligations are about $52 bn.

Blackstone-backed AirTrunk postponed a $1.5 bn REIT IPO, and even at a 6% yield found no takers. With USTs at 5.2%, capital-intensive AI infra expansion is colliding with a funding freeze, making the 'model–cloud–chips' excess-returns trilemma increasingly explicit. At a pre-IPO investor meeting, Anthropic disclosed Q3 revenue of $16.8 bn, up nearly 46% QoQ, with adj. profitability and positive FCF for the quarter. Returns on compute outlays have improved, with $1 of compute cost driving $1.7 of revenue.

This validates the commercialization capability of frontier models and paves the way for its IPO. However, QoQ growth slowed notably vs. earlier periods and fell short of some expectations, and adj. profit is not GAAP net income.

In a landscape of ongoing AI price wars and higher rates weighing on multiples, this profitability proof-point is a key benchmark, while forcing a rethink of the growth ceiling for big models and the ROI on compute capex. Apple will roll out China-localized Apple Intelligence in Dec, partnering with Alibaba and BIDU. The initial features (Genmoji, notification summary, etc.) will launch domestically via an iOS update, with compliance safeguards co-built with Alibaba and search/Siri localization via BIDU.

Regulatory clearance for onshore AI gives Apple a differentiated edge in its largest market. Alibaba and BIDU gain distribution into on-device AI, creating a three-way win, though near-term hardware lift should be limited. Netflix announced a global headcount reduction of about 1,000, or 6% of staff, its largest since 2022. Cuts focus on product, tech, legal, HR and other G&A functions, and the company said full-year profitability guidance remains unchanged, with resources refocused on higher-value initiatives.

With TikTok and YouTube UGC continuing to siphon viewing time, the layoffs signal cost optimization and tighter opex control. The market reads this as a sign of growth anxiety and will look to the Oct 20 print for validation on subs, engagement, and ad-tier metrics; near term this should lift margins, but core growth challenges persist. content: U.S.-listed shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) fell 1.7% in overnight trading ahead of Thursday despite a strong quarterly report from the world’s biggest contract chip manufacturer. Chip stocks in the U.S. and Asia remained under pressure on Thursday, extending the selloff from the past few days, amid fresh concerns about the durability of AI infrastructure spending and chip demand, which also pressured TSM stock. Early Thursday, TSM forecast that its fourth-quarter revenue would rise as much as 61% from a year ago, after posting a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings. The Taiwanese company’s net profit in the July-to-September period rose 69% to T$763.1 billion ($23.59 billion), beating LSEG SmartEstimate expectations of T$746.3 billion. TSMC’s third-quarter revenue rose 51% to T$1.49 trillion, beating market forecasts, according to a disclosure last week. In dollar terms, sales rose 41%. Over the past year, TSMC raised its 2026 revenue growth outlook to “slightly above 40%” in dollar terms. With semiconductor firms ASML Holding NV (AMSL) and Samsung Electronics reporting strong results in recent weeks, TSMC's report allays fears of a slowdown in booming AI infrastructure spending. Still, broader concerns related to AI returns continue to weigh across tech stocks. NVDA was down 1.4% in overnight trading, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) dipped nearly 2% on Wednesday, its sixth straight session of decline. South Korea’s KOSPI dropped 7.5% on Thursday, with sharp declines in SK Hynix and Samsung. TSM shares also came under pressure amid the global rout. The stock fell in six of the last seven sessions through Wednesday, losing 11.5% cumulatively. Reports of advances by Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) have raised fears of tougher competition for U.S. chip firms, while Broadcom CEO Hock Tan’s recent warning likening AI investments to “casino gambling” has added to questions about whether the massive spending on AI infrastructure will pay off. TSM was the top trending stock on Stocktwits at the time of writing, with retail sentiment climbing multiple points higher in the ‘bullish’ zone. “$TSM between this and the news about Anthropic's revenue, it’s going to be a Green Day tomorrow for AI/tech stocks,” a trader said. Anthropic reportedly disclosed its financial performance to select investors on Wednesday, showing third-quarter sales of $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in Q2 and $4.7 billion in Q1. “$TSM another massively good report and we seem to be completely risk off this week,” said another trader. Despite the recent weakness, TSM stock remains 42.4% up year to date. Certaines données de marché sont fournies par ICE Data Services. Certaines données de référence sont fournies par FactSet. title: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufactur (TSM) Q3 FY2026 earnings call transcript - Yahoo Finance
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results TSMC delivered Q3 2026 revenue of $46.7B, up 16.2% QoQ and above guidance, with gross margin at 66.4% despite dilution from 2nm ramp. Management guided Q4 revenue to $52.3–$54.3B (up 14% QoQ, 58% YoY at midpoint) and expects full-year 2026 revenue growth of ~44% YoY, driven by robust AI and advanced node demand. Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to TSMC's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. This is Jeff Su, TSMC's Director of Investor Relations and your host for today. TSMC is hosting our earnings conference call via live audio webcast through the company's website at www.tsmc.com, where you can also download the earnings release materials. If you are joining us through the conference call, your dial-in lines are in listen-only mode. The format for today's event will be as follows. First, TSMC's Senior Vice President, third quarter 2026, followed by our guidance for the fourth quarter 2026. Then Mr. Huang and TSMC's Chairman and CEO, Dr. C.C. Wei, will jointly provide the company's key messages. Then we will open the line for the Q&A session. As usual, I would like to remind everybody that today's discussions may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to significant risk and uncertainties, which could cause the actual results to differ materially from those contained in the forward-looking statements. Please refer to the safe harbor notice that appears in our press release. Now, I would like to turn the call over to TSMC CFO, Mr. Wendell Huang, for the summary of operations and the current quarter guidance. Thank you, Jeff. Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. My presentation will start with financial highlights for the third quarter of 2026. After that, I will provide the guidance for the fourth quarter of 2026. Third quarter revenue increased 17.6% sequentially in NT, supported by strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies. In U.S. dollar term, revenue increased 16.2% sequentially to $46.7 billion, above the high end of our third-quarter guidance. Gross margin decreased by 1.3 percentage points sequentially to 66.4%, primarily due to margin dilution from 2 nm ramp. Total operating expenses accounted for 7.8% of net revenue. Operating margin was 58.7%. Overall, our third-quarter EPS reached TWD 29.43 and ROE was 45.5%. Now, let's move on to revenue by technology. 2 nm process technology contributed 8% of wafer revenue in the third quarter, while 3 nm, 5 nm, and 7 nm accounted for 33%, 28%, and 10% respectively. Advanced technologies, defined as 7 nm and below, accounted for 79% of wafer revenue. Moving on to revenue contribution by platform. HPC increased 22% quarter-over-quarter to account for 68% of our third-quarter revenue. Smartphone increased 10% to account for 21%. IoT increased 5% to account for 4%. Automotive increased 23% to account for 4%, while DCE declined 12% to account for 1%. Moving on to the balance sheet. We ended the third quarter with cash and marketable securities of TWD 4 trillion, or $126 billion. On the liability side, current liabilities increased by TWD 110 billion quarter-over-quarter, mainly due to the increase of TWD 46 billion in current portions of bond payable and bank loans and TWD 26 billion in dividend payable. In terms of financial ratios, accounts receivable turnover days decreased by 1-28 days. Inventory days decreased by 5-82 days, primarily due to the increase in wafer shipment. Regarding cash flow and CapEx, during the third quarter, we generated about TWD 920 billion in cash from operations, spent TWD 443 billion in CapEx, and distributed TWD 156 billion for fourth quarter 2025 cash dividends. Overall, our cash balance increased TWD 488 billion-TWD 3.6 trillion at the end of the quarter. In U.S. dollar terms, our third-quarter capital expenditures totaled $13.8 billion. I have finished my financial summary. Now, let's turn to our current quarter guidance. Based on the current business outlook, we expect our fourth quarter revenue to be between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, which represents a 14% sequential increase or a 58% year-over-year increase at the midpoint. Based on the exchange rate assumption of one U.S. dollar to TWD 31.8, gross margin is expected to be between 65% and 67%, operating margin between 56.5% and 58.5%. This concludes my financial presentation. Now, let me turn to our key messages. I will start by talking about our third quarter 2026 and fourth quarter of 2026 profitability. Compared to second quarter, our third quarter gross margin decreased by 130 basis points sequentially to 66.4%, primarily due to the margin dilution from the initial ramp-up of our 2 nm technology. We have just guided our fourth quarter gross margin to decrease by 40 basis points to 66% at the midpoint, primarily due to the continued margin dilution from the steep ramp-up of our 2 nm technology, as well as dilution from overseas fabs. These impacts are expected to be partially offset by cost improvement efforts, including productivity gains and across node capacity optimization. While the cost of overseas fabs remain higher, thanks to the company's overall larger scale and cost improvement efforts, we now expect the gross margin dilution from the ramp-up of our overseas fabs to be closer to 2% more effort to support the strong structural demand from our customers. More fabs will be ramping up in the U.S. Thus, we expect the dilution from our overseas fabs to widen to 3%-4% in the next few years. We will leverage our increasing size in Arizona and work on our operations to improve the cost structure. We will also continue to work closely with our customers and suppliers to manage the impact. Overall, with our fundamental competitive advantages of manufacturing technology leadership and large-scale production base, we are confident that TSMC continues to be the most cost-efficient manufacturer in every region that we operate. Next, let me make some comments on our 2026 capital budget. At TSMC, a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years. Given the continued robust multi-year demand from our customers, including the emerging agentic AI market, we reiterate our full year 2026 capital budget to be between $60 billion and $64 billion. We continue to expect our CapEx investment from 2026 to 2028 to be even more significantly higher than the past three years as we continue to invest heavily to support our customers' growth. Additionally, while the tool supply is tight, we always collaborate closely with our tool suppliers well in advance to prepare the capacity, just like our customers collaborate with us well in advance to plan our capacity. Even as we invest for the future growth with this level of CapEx spending in the next few years, we remain committed to delivering profitable growth to our shareholders. We also remain committed to a sustainable and steadily increasing cash dividend per share on both an annual and quarterly basis. Now, let me turn the microphone over to C.C. Thank you, Wendell. Good afternoon, everyone. First, let me start with our near-term demand outlook. We concluded our third quarter with a revenue of $46.7 billion, higher than our guidance in U.S. dollar terms, driven by strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies. Moving into fourth quarter 2026, we expect our business to be supported by continued strong demand for our leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2 nm technology. Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end market segment are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties. As such, we are being prudent in our business planning going into 2027 while focusing on the fundamentals of our business to further strengthen our competitive position. Having said that, demand for our leading-edge technologies continue to be extremely robust, supported by our strong technology differentiation and broader customer base. Therefore, we now expect our full year 2026 revenue growth to be around 44% year-over-year in U.S. dollar term. Next, let me talk about the AI-related demand outlook. The AI market continues to be very strong. Recent developments are very positive to AI's long-term demand outlook. We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance. In addition, we are observing great adoption of open source AI models. This will drive greater efficiency and help lower the barrier to future AI usage, and result in more and more demand for leading-edge silicon. Thus, AI-related demand is being supported by strong underlying demand for AI accelerators. In addition, the emergence of agentic AI CPUs and the continued demand for networking chips are driving further silicon demand. Therefore, semiconductor will remain essential in the AI mega trend. The value of semiconductors in the global supply chain is set to continue to increase in our view. This will create more value opportunities for our customers to capture and more value opportunities for TSMC as well. No matter which approach is taken, you will require use of the most advanced semiconductor process technology. With our technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust, we are well-positioned to capture the full multi-year structural AI-related demand. Therefore, all the AI players are working with TSMC. Next, let me talk about TSMC's capacity expansion strategy. As a foundry, our first responsibility is to provide our customer with the best technologies and effective capacity support to unleash their innovations. To address the structured increase in the long-term semiconductor market demand profile, TSMC collaborate closely with our customers, yet our customer's customer to plan for our capacity. In addition, we are now going one step further and sending our own teams of people to check on the data center build-out progress and power supply situation in the U.S. The feedback is so far so good, and the CSPs has been well-prepared. Internally, TSMC employed a disciplined capacity planning system to assess the market demand from both a top-down and bottom-up approach. This is a continuous and ongoing process. Given the fundamental complexity of leading-edge technologies and the design in and lead time involved, we already have a very good idea of customers' multi-year product roadmap and production plans. Thus, we continue to hold strong conviction in the AI mega trend. We are moving full speed ahead to increase our capacity to meet our assessed demand, and stepping up our CapEx investment to support our customers' future growth. TSMC is expanding at unprecedented pace with a nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress. We are building 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fab in Taiwan over the next several years, and another five to six fabs overseas. Our new node, N2, has already entered high-volume manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025 with good yield. N2 is ramping successfully in multiple phases at both Hsinchu and Kaohsiung site. We expect our N2 family technologies annual capacity to more than double in 2027, supported by strong demand from both smartphone and HPC AI applications. We are also leveraging our manufacturing excellence to generate more N2 wafer output, further increasing our capacity support to customers. In addition, we have already begun preparing the capacity for our A14 technology. Risk production is well on track for 2027, and volume production will start in 2028. Thus, TSMC's semiconductor technologies and manufacturing will continue to play a pivotal role in supporting the global semiconductor industry while unleashing our customers' innovation. Now, let me talk about TSMC's global N3 capacity expansion update. As we said before, historically, we do not add additional capacity to a node once it reaches its targeted capacity. However, based on our assessment, we are executing well on our global capacity plan to add three new fabs to support the robust multi-year pipeline or demand for 3 nm technologies. In Taiwan, volume production for our new 3 nm fab in Tainan Science Park is well on track to begin the first half of 2027. In addition, driven by the strong demand from our customer, we have decided to add one additional 3 nm fab in Tainan. Volume production is scheduled for the first half of 2028. In Arizona, we have completed the construction of our second fab and are in the process of tool moving and installation. Volume production will begin in third quarter 2027, slightly ahead of our previous schedule. In Japan, we are progressing well to our plan to utilize 3 nm in our second fab, and volume production is scheduled in 2028. In addition to all the new fabs, we continue to convert 5 nm tool to support 3 nm capacity in Taiwan. We are also leveraging our manufacturing excellence to greater productivity across our fab in all locations. To generate more wafer output, we are also focusing on capacity optimization across nodes, which including flexible capacity support among N7, N5, and N3 node. Thus, we are using multiple levers to do everything we can, whenever we can, as fast as we can, to maximize the support to our customers. We have no intention to leave food on the table for others, and we want to capture every piece of business possible. This concluding our key message, and thank you for your attention. Thank you, C.C. This concludes our prepared statements. Before we begin the question-and-answer session, I would like to remind everybody to please limit your questions to two at a time to allow as many participants as possible the opportunity to ask their questions. Should you wish to raise your question in Chinese, I will translate it to English before our management answers your question. For those of you on the call, if you would like to ask a question, please press the star then one on your telephone keypad now. If at any time you'd like to remove yourself from the questioning queue, please press star two. Now, let's begin the Q&A session. Operator, can we proceed with the first caller on the line, please? Yes. First one, Laura Chen, Citi. Go ahead, please. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, and appreciate C.C. for sharing with us the TSMC capacity expansion strategy. May I follow up more on that? Given the increasing aggressive AI semiconductor demand, how does TSMC now see the AI revenue CAGR growth, and how does TSMC reconcile customer the capacity requirement with some of the potential concern on the data center power availability, and also maybe funding recently and other critical components such as the HBM, APS, advanced packaging, and also in the networking side, we see the tightness of laser as well. If these kind of trends create a mismatch between semiconductor supply and also actual AI development, how would TSMC adjust your capa-minimize the potential overbuilding in the supply chain? Again, our CapEx will be much higher than today. You are talking about the gross margin or the profitability can be increased or not. Higher, sorry. What was the last part of your question, Sunny? Higher tool price, higher what? Sunny, thank you very much. If I may have a very quick follow-up on the CapEx side. Okay, Sunny's question is about the puts and takes to next year's margin. C.C. did say we are pulling in the schedule for the second fab for 3 nm. Her question is, are we also pulling in third fab? What's leading to this wider dilution? Maybe, yeah. As we mentioned, we are doing everything we can wherever we can to increase our capacity to meet the strong demand from the customers. You mentioned in the prepared remarks that the AI accelerator chipset demand is proliferating into agentic AI demand, including CPUs and networking switches. We understand the overall AI investment is still pretty strong and even trending stronger across the board. Does that increase the complexity of the node process architecture, make the learning curve more challenging or difficult, and therefore the implication to the margin? Well, today's situation actually is a little bit different from previous years. Yes, we now have a very strong demand from smartphone and also AI HPC applications. So the smaller die size per se or the big die size in the accelerator, they happen at the same time. This is to TSMC's advantage, let me say that. Because we are good. We have been prepared for this kind of thing, and happy to working with us. So the learning curve, yes, but we are doing a reasonable job, and so the customer are very happy today. Okay. Thank you. title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom - CNBC
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips. Here are TSMC’s third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate: The world’s largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier. TSMC’s third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company’s earnings call. The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand. TSMC’s stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company’s elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email. TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process. Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC’s careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems. “Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity,” he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers’ ability to deploy the chips they order. Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC’s total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips. By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate. TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors. The company’s free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago. TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain. TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule. TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona. The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence. TSMC makes cutting-edge semiconductors for the likes of Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and components for Apple. The biggest buyers of those chips – including cloud companies Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft – have set aside $725 billion for AI-related investments this year. The latest performance shows steady demand for advanced chips, which power data centers and other systems that power AI applications, smartphones and automobiles. In April, the Taiwanese giant raised its full-year sales guidance and said its capital spending should trend toward the upper end of an existing forecast range of up to $56 billion in 2026. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced in May that the U.S. chip designer would set up a headquarters in Taiwan and invest up to $150 billion annually in the region. Still, TSMC CEO C.C. Wei had warned in June that his company won’t be able to meet demand from American customers for years, even as more manufacturing capacity comes online in the U.S. over the next few years. (HIMS) are turning investor attention toward peptides after its roughest week in two months, as it launches a new consumer campaign just days before a closely watched FDA advisory meeting. HIMS stock declined 7% last week, with shares also down over 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Late Sunday, HIMS published an Instagram carousel explaining what peptides are, why they have attracted biohackers and how they could become part of mainstream healthcare. The campaign comes as investors search for Hims’ next major growth engine beyond compounded GLP-1 drugs, and as regulators prepare to decide whether seven popular peptides should receive a clearer pathway into the U.S. compounding market. Hims said more than 170 peptides are in active clinical development, presenting the category as established science rather than a passing wellness trend. “Peptides aren’t new—they’ve been researched for decades,” the post said. “What’s changed? Research is growing, and peptides are becoming part of mainstream health conversations.” The final slide also acknowledged one of the market’s biggest challenges: inconsistent sourcing and formulation. “Not all peptides are created equal,” Hims said. “The science is real. Quality is what makes the difference.” The campaign comes ahead of the FDA’s July 23-24 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting, where members will consider adding BPC-157, Emideltide, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and TB-500 to the Section 503A Bulks List. FDA staff have recommended against all seven, citing limited human evidence, unclear formulations and unresolved risks including immune reactions and contamination. Former committee member Dr. Anita Gupta said earlier reviews raised “some red flags” over immunogenicity and pointed to reports of “heavy metals,” “microbial contamination” and mislabeling. The Partnership for Safe Medicines also urged rejection, saying the evidence is dominated by animal studies, laboratory research and weak overseas trials. It noted that BPC-157 has fewer than 36 human participants across three studies, KPV has no live-human trials and TB-500 has only one human tolerance study. The group also warned that compounding could falsely signal FDA approval and cited 127 peptide shipments entering U.S. ports in the first quarter, with about 39% coming from manufacturers outside FDA oversight. That stance contrasts with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s push for a looser approach. Kennedy has said peptides worked on his injuries with “really good effect,” while 12 peptides were moved into Category 1 in April, an early step toward possible pharmacy compounding. Shares of Circle (CRCL) were on track to hit a monthly high on pre-market trade on Friday following a dip to an over three-month low in the previous trading session. The uptick came after the company announced it had received final approval from the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to establish First National Digital Currency Bank. The final approval marks the end of a process that began in December 2025, when Circle first received conditional approval alongside Ripple (XRP), BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets, and Paxos. It will operate as Circle National Trust, a national trust bank that brings stablecoin USDC's (USDC) custody infrastructure under direct federal oversight. CRCL’s stock jumped 13% in pre-market trade, on track to hit its highest level in July and climb back above the $70-mark. It was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. The stock price had hit an over three-month low of under $62 in the previous session, after which Ark Invest’s Cathie Wood picked up 217,896 shares. Circle’s partner for the USDC stablecoin, Coinbase (COIN), also saw its shares rally. COIN’s stock rose nearly 5% in the pre-market trade, and was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits. Coinbase received conditional approval from the OCC to establish Coinbase National Trust Company in April, earlier this year. However, while Circle saw retail sentiment pivot to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ territory over the past day, sentiment around Coinbase stayed in the ‘bearish’ zone. Sentiment around USDC remained in ‘neutral’ territory. The rally in both crypto-linked stocks also came as Bitcoin (BTC) climbed back above $64,000. BTC’s price rose over 2.5% in the last 24 hours, leading to an uptick in the shares of companies like Michael Saylor-backed Strategy (MSTR) and others. Once fully operational, Circle National Trust will provide fiduciary digital asset custody services for Circle and its affiliates, with plans to eventually extend custody services to institutional customers such as banks and regulated derivatives organizations. The charter also lays the groundwork for a future capability like bringing management of the USDC Reserve under direct federal oversight. Circle's charter was one of two de novo national trust bank applications the OCC approved in this cycle, alongside Ripple National Trust Bank, while BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets, and Paxos converted existing state trust charters into national ones. Anchorage Digital was the only crypto firm to hold this type of federal charter previously, having secured it in 2021. Industry trade groups have pushed back on the wave of approvals, with the Bank Policy Institute stating the OCC's conditions "leave substantial unanswered questions," while the Independent Community Bankers of America argued the charter type was being "stretched beyond its statutory and historical purpose." Shares of Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN) and Oracle Corp. (ORCL) were in focus on Friday after the U.K. government designated the four companies as Critical Third Parties (CTPs) to strengthen and safeguard the country’s financial systems. At the time of writing, MSFT stock was up 0.4%, ORCL shares climbed 1%, while GOOG and AMZN shares edged 0.2% lower each. The firms covered under the new framework are Microsoft Ireland Operations, Google Cloud EMEA, Amazon Web Services EMEA, and Oracle Corporation UK. Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will jointly oversee the critical services the four companies provide to the financial sector. The aim is to reduce the risk of widespread disruption if a major cloud provider experiences operational issues. Regulatory oversight will apply only to the financial sector, not to their broader business operations. The designated companies will be required to maintain strong systems to identify, manage, and recover from disruptions affecting services used by financial institutions. Regulators will also be allowed to gather information, assess operational resilience, and, when necessary, introduce or enforce CTP-specific rules to ensure the continuity of critical services. “These designations will help ensure the critical services financial firms rely on remain resilient, protecting consumers and businesses while supporting growth across the economy,” said Rachel Blake, Economic Secretary to the Treasury of the United Kingdom. Meanwhile, gross margin for the quarter came in at 66%, operating margin reached 58%, and net profit margin stood at 51%. HPC continued to dominate the company’s revenue mix. The segment accounted for 61% of total revenue, underscoring its role as TSM’s largest growth engine, as AI-related workloads drive strong semiconductor demand. Smartphones contributed 26% of revenue, while IoT accounted for 6% and automotive for 4%.
